analysis.one_liner: Raises car fuel economy standards to 35 mpg and mandates renewable fuels and efficiency standards for appliances and lighting.
analysis.headline: It became law on December 19, 2007, passing the Senate 86-8 and the House 314-100 — but only after Senate Republicans blocked, 53-42 on a 60-vote procedural test, the version that had passed the House and repealed oil and gas industry tax breaks.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill started as an attempt to take away tax breaks and royalty relief from oil and gas companies and use the money for renewable energy. Along the way it grew into a much larger energy law: it requires cars and trucks to average 35 miles per gallon by 2020, forces a rising amount of renewable fuel (mostly ethanol) into the gasoline supply through 2022, sets efficiency standards for light bulbs and appliances, trains workers for energy-efficiency jobs, and pools against drowning with new swimming-pool drain safety rules. The oil company tax increases that anchored the original House bill were dropped after Senate Republicans blocked the bill in December 2007.
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers save on fuel as the fleet average must reach 35 mpg by 2020; homeowners get weatherization help and cheaper-to-run appliances and light bulbs; workers get green-job training programs; and biofuel producers, battery makers, and auto manufacturers gain a guaranteed renewable-fuel market plus up to $25 billion in low-cost federal loans for retooling plants [S5][S6].

how_it_helps.text: Requires the combined new-car fleet to average at least 35 miles per gallon by model year 2020, replacing the long-standing 27.5 mpg requirement, with standards continuing to rise through 2030 [S5][S6].
Requires increasing volumes of renewable fuel in transportation fuel each year through 2022, with lifecycle greenhouse gas reduction requirements for new facilities [S5].
Sets first-ever federal efficiency standards for general service light bulbs and updates standards for appliances, boilers, motors, and consumer electronics [S5][S6].
Reauthorizes and expands the weatherization assistance program for low-income households through 2012 [S5].

Creates a green-jobs worker training program under the Workforce Investment Act and requires up to $25 billion in loans for advanced vehicle manufacturing, with prevailing-wage requirements for construction work [S5][S6].
Includes the Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act, requiring anti-entrapment drain covers to prevent drownings [S6].
Prohibits market manipulation and false price reporting in wholesale petroleum markets, enforceable by the FTC with civil penalties [S5].

analysis.who_pays: In the original House version, oil and gas companies bore the cost through the loss of a major tax deduction, longer write-off periods, and new fees and royalty requirements on offshore leases [S2][S3]. In the final law, taxpayers fund the authorized grant, loan, and research programs, and consumers pay somewhat higher upfront prices for cars, bulbs, and appliances, offset over time by energy savings [S5][S6].
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers and buyers of cars and appliances

drawbacks.text: The renewable fuel mandate guarantees demand for ethanol whether or not it delivers, and the law itself directs a National Academy of Sciences study of its impact on feed grains, livestock, food, and forest products — an acknowledgment that the mandate could raise food and feed costs [S5].

Tighter fuel economy and appliance standards raise the sticker price of new cars, appliances, and light bulbs; the savings come later in lower energy bills, which costs more for households that cannot afford the newer products.
Much of the law is studies, grant authorizations, and advisory committees rather than guaranteed spending, so many provisions depend on later appropriations [S5][S6].

The title that would have ended oil and gas tax benefits and rolled back offshore royalty relief — and funded a Strategic Energy Efficiency and Renewables Reserve with the proceeds — was dropped entirely, so the renewable and efficiency programs were never paid for by the industry the original bill targeted [S3][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On balance this was a consequential law for ordinary households: the 35 mpg standard and the lighting and appliance rules deliver real, lasting fuel and utility savings, and the pool safety title prevents child drownings. But it is a badly lopsided bargain in one respect: the version enacted never paid for its programs through the oil industry tax repeal the House had passed, and its biofuel title entrenches corn ethanol with a guaranteed market whose costs and climate benefits were uncertain enough that Congress ordered a study of its effect on food prices. The vehicle standards apply to automakers, but taxpayers also lend the same automakers up to $25 billion to comply.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate version with the oil-and-gas tax increase died on a 60-vote procedural vote that fell short 53-42, so Democratic leaders dropped that title; the remaining bill passed the Senate 86-8 and the House 314-100 and was signed into law.

narrative.text: The House passed the original bill on January 18, 2007, 264-163, with 228 of 233 Democrats in favor and only 36 of 202 Republicans; the bill denied oil companies the domestic production tax deduction, lengthened the write-off period for geological expenditures, and rolled back offshore royalty relief [S3][S9][S12].
The Senate stripped the oil and gas tax and royalty titles and added biofuel mandates, fuel economy standards, and efficiency provisions, passing its version 65-27 in June 2007 [S4][S15].
In December 2007 the House passed a compromise that restored the oil company tax title, 235-181, with 221 of 233 Democrats in favor [S16].
Senate Republicans blocked that version: cloture, the 60-vote test to end a filibuster, failed 53-42, with only 5 of 49 Republicans in favor [S17].
A second attempt with an amendment also failed cloture 59-40, short of 60 [S18].
After the tax title was dropped, the Senate passed the remaining bill 86-8, with 40 of 49 Republicans voting yes, and the House followed 314-100 on December 18 [S19][S20].
President Bush signed it on December 19, 2007, as Public Law 110-140 [S8][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies are better off because the tax and royalty provisions that had passed the House were stripped out before the law was signed. Ethanol and biofuel producers gained a guaranteed market through 2022, and automakers gained access to up to $25 billion in low-cost federal loans. Consumers still gained the fuel economy and appliance efficiency standards.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies, ethanol producers, and automakers

for.name: 228 of 233 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on passage in January, yes on the December compromise that restored the oil tax title, and yes on final passage [S9][S12][S16][S20].

for.name: Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Moved the bill to the floor (91-0 cloture on the motion to proceed), passed their version 65-27 in June, and passed the final bill 44-1 in December [S13][S15][S19].

for.name: President George W. Bush
for.what_they_did: Signed the bill into law on December 19, 2007 [S8][S5].

against.name: 159 of 202 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on passage in January and against the December compromise that included the oil company tax title (14 of 199 in favor) [S12][S16].

against.name: 39 of 49 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted against cloture on the December version containing the oil and gas tax title, defeating the 60-vote test 53-42 [S17].

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Major oil companies and trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed the tax and royalty provisions and campaigned against them during the Senate debate.

sides.party_line_note: The early votes split sharply by party — the House passed it 264-163 with 228 of 233 Democrats and only 36 of 202 Republicans — and the December fight over the oil tax title was nearly all Democrats (46 of 49) versus Republicans (5 of 49); once that title was dropped, final passage was bipartisan, 86-8 in the Senate and 314-100 in the House with 95 Republicans in favor [S9][S12][S16][S17][S19][S20].

industries.note: The House version would have denied them the domestic production tax deduction, stretched their geological write-offs from five to seven years, and rolled back offshore royalty relief and other Gulf lease breaks [S2][S3]. The final law kept only the longer amortization period, so they shed a modest cost while keeping the larger tax benefits, which ordinary taxpayers effectively backstop [S5].

The renewable fuel standard mandates rising volumes of renewable fuel in the gasoline supply through 2022, creating a guaranteed customer base enforced by federal credit rules [S5][S6]. Consumers bear the mandate at the pump and, potentially, in food and feed prices — a risk Congress itself ordered studied [S5].

They must reach a combined 35 mpg fleet average by 2020, a real compliance cost, but the same law gives them grants and up to $25 billion in low-cost federal loans to retool, with prevailing-wage requirements for construction [S5][S6].
New federal efficiency standards for light bulbs and appliances force product redesigns, but with multi-year phase-ins and R&D prize programs to help develop replacements [S5][S6].

Solar, geothermal, marine, battery, and smart grid programs receive research funding, grants, and loan guarantees, and the advanced battery loan guarantee program supports U.S. battery manufacturing [S5][S6].
